extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and workshop participants who want to write characters unlike themselves
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and exercises for creating plausible, non-stereotyped fictional characters who differ from the author in race, orientation, age, ability, religion, sex, and similar traits; includes classroom-tested techniques for noticing and revising unexamined bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depart from the dominant paradigm / unmarked state
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that most fiction defaults to a cultural 'dominant paradigm' or 'unmarked state' (commonly white, male, heterosexual, young, physically able, etc.) and deliberately depart from that default when creating characters who are 'other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the unmarked state's effects on reader assumptions (example: telling a river-crossing story with a default 'someone' vs. 'a pregnant woman' changes reader inference). If your characters are in marked states, depict how readers (and other characters) would notice and respond; avoid accidentally treating marked characters as if they occupy the unmarked state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the ROAARS framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus attention on the specific categories the guide highlights—Race / (sexual) Orientation / Age / Ability / Religion / Sex (ROAARS)—as the kinds of differences most emphasized by majority culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The acronym helps prioritize which traits are likely to be 'marked' in most cultural contexts. Note the deliberate omission of class in ROAARS and the implications of that omission for representation and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and research who has privilege and when
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn through observation and research which groups have privilege in given contexts and when that privilege applies, so your characters' experiences align with realistic social dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: legal status of same-sex marriage (as of 2005) affects whether gay couples can marry; 'Driving While Black' and 'Driving While White' examples show differential policing. Failure to represent who notices privilege (or would reasonably notice it) is a common mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on clichés and stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not default to useful clichés or stereotypical traits when depicting characters different from you; such shortcuts produce implausible or offensive representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises and rewrites should surface where you 'clung to useful clichés.' Use revision and research to replace stereotypes with specific, grounded detail. The guide emphasizes that many mistakes result from unconsidered thoughts shaped by cultural messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and override reptile brain / lazy forebrain reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that instinctive pattern-recognition ('reptile brain') and a lazy, routinized conscious mind ('lazy forebrain') can generate prejudiced thoughts or snap judgments; these must be caught and corrected during writing and revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide explains how the reptile brain learns bad information from society and feeds it to conscious thought; writers should use conscious critical thinking and revision to override these automatic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite to diversify characters (especially secondary cast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rewrites to develop secondary characters who might initially default to being similar to the author; deliberately change them so they are not all straight, middle-class, unreligious white adults similar to the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide reports that initial creative drafts commonly produce characters similar to the author's unmarked state; purposeful revision 'changes these characters enormously' and improves plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice timed 'hothouse forcing' exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Use timed exercises (the guide recommends trying them at least once) to force immediate writing from perspectives unlike your own, which helps bypass the internal editor and surface raw material to be revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises are not tests and cannot be failed; they often work best with partners or groups but can be done alone. Example Exercise 1: pick a celebrity, pretend to be them, and write a description of a person with a very different ROAARS in four minutes; then reflect on what surfaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes are fixable—try anyway
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not avoid writing about people unlike themselves out of fear of getting it horribly or offensively wrong; making mistakes is part of the process and errors can be corrected through revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide reassures writers that a single ignorant thought does not make them a racist or bigot permanently; writing gives opportunity to 'rewrite and revise' and to override automatic prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't presume cross-difference expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Being different from the dominant paradigm in one respect (e.g., race) does not make you an expert about other kinds of differences (e.g., disability, religion); avoid assuming competence across categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note explicitly that 'difference is not monolithic' and that each marked trait requires its own awareness, research, and care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray awareness (or lack thereof) of privilege believably
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character is marked in a given context, they will likely notice instances of privilege that unmarked characters would not; conversely, it is implausible for marked characters to fail to notice privileges that affect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives examples (e.g., slave characters not noticing freedom of owners would be implausible) and advises ensuring that characters' awareness matches what is socially probable for their position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent state changes realistically
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict transitions between marked and unmarked states (people marry, change class, discover sexual orientation, change religion, undergo gender transitions, acquire disabilities, etc.) because such changes affect how characters are perceived and what privileges they have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide lists many ways people can move between states (marriage, moving, surgery, discovering ancestry) and stresses that fictional people also change; account for these dynamic aspects when plotting and characterizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classroom-style workshop methods and peer exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate workshop techniques—partner/group exercises, timed writings, and reflection—to train noticing and revision habits that improve depiction of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format guidance: do all exercises at least once; many work best in groups though not required; exercises are designed for writing action rather than prolonged thinking; suggested completion times are provided.
